value.text: Fix a real mean-zero q in H^gamma and assume L1: ||q||_(H^gamma)<=R. H001-H003 give T>0, 0<gamma<=1 and R>0. Use E001 for source datum U0(x)=-q(-x), exponent s=gamma and horizon T. Reflection and sign preserve the Fourier Sobolev and L2 norms, so ||U0||_(dot H^gamma)<=R and ||U0||_2<=R. The source yields a global unique continuous flow, its uniform Sobolev bound, and smooth flows when the datum is smooth (apply its positive regularity statements for each integer exponent in that case). Its Galerkin bound and limiting-solution bound are uniform for the prescribed norm bounds.

Take that source flow U and set u(t,x)=-U(t,-x). At (t,-x), u_t=-U_t, u_x=U_x and u_xxx=U_xxx, so u_t+u_xxx=-U U_x=u*u_x. Fourier coefficients are hat u(k)=-hat U(-k), preserving reality, zero mean and every Fourier norm. On mean-zero functions and s>=0, |k|<=<k><=sqrt(2)|k|, hence ||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s); for s<0 the inequalities reverse as in the supplied norm convention. The source bound therefore gives some A(T,gamma,R) in our norm. It also holds for a smooth-approximation limit by passing first in each finite Fourier norm sum and then taking the supremum over finite sets. The sign-reflection map is invertible, so uniqueness and continuous dependence transfer. Finally differentiation of v=S_(-t)u cancels the linear KdV term and yields v'=B_t(v,v)/2 for smooth data; the unimodular Fourier symbol of S preserves all norms. Thus M=1+sup||v||_(H^gamma)<=1+A as asserted. This proves the asserted existence, bound, twist identity and solution convention for arbitrary q under L1; discharge L1.

For arbitrary real mean-zero L2 data q1,q2 and B0>=0, temporarily assume L2: ||q1||_2+||q2||_2<=B0. Apply E001's theta=0 dependence statement at time horizon T to -q1(-x),-q2(-x). Their norms and their difference norm are unchanged. The source twists are unitary, so its dependence bound gives sup_[0,T]||u_q1-u_q2||_2<=C(T,B0)||q1-q2||_2 in physical variables after sign-reflection. Discharge L2.

Fix tau>0 and real alpha,beta. If either phase is zero, substitution in eta shows exact cancellation. Otherwise put h(s)=exp(-i*alpha*s)-M_tau(exp(-i*alpha*s)). The covariance is tau^(-1)integral_0^tau h(s)exp(-i*beta*s)ds. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, |exp(-i*alpha*s)-exp(-i*alpha*r)|<=|alpha||s-r|. Averaging in r gives |h(s)|<=tau|alpha|, and consequently |eta|<=tau|alpha|. Interchange alpha,beta to obtain the minimum. Also |h(0)|+|h(tau)|<=tau|alpha| and integral_0^tau|h'(s)|ds=tau|alpha|. Integrating the beta exponential once by parts gives |eta|<=(|h(0)|+|h(tau)|+integral|h'|)/(tau|beta|)<=2|alpha/beta|. Interchanging phases proves the other ratio. These arguments apply to smooth scalar exponentials, so the calculus identities have no limiting issue.

Fix nonzero integer frequencies a,b,c,d with sum zero, order their magnitudes N1>=N2>=N3>=N4, and put A=|ab|, B0=|cd|. Triangle inequality gives N1<=3N2. For the first majorant, if d is among the largest two, min(A/B0,B0/A)<=1 and 1/|d|<=1/N3. Otherwise the two largest are among a,b,c. If they are a,b, use (B0/A)/|d|=|c|/|ab|<=1/N3. If they are a,c, their ratio lies in [1/3,3], giving (1/|d|)min(A/B0,B0/A)<=3 min(|b|/|d|^2,1/|b|)<=3/max(|b|,|d|)=3/N3; the last inequality follows by dividing into |b|<=|d| and its complement. The b,c case is the identical exchange of a,b. For the second majorant, if the largest two lie in a single pair (a,b) or (c,d), the other pair sum has magnitude <=2N3, whereas max(A,B0)>=N1N2>=N3^2. Since a+b=-(c+d), the ratio is <=2/N3. If they lie in different pairs, the third largest is paired with one of them, so max(A,B0)>=N2N3 while |a+b|<=2N1<=6N2. This gives 6/N3. Ties admit any ordering and the cases still exhaust all possibilities.

Fix four finitely supported nonnegative sequences x1,x2,x3,x4 on Z\{0}. Decompose each into shells 2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1), j>=0, and let X_(r,j) be its ell2 norm on shell j. Fix one ordering of shell indices j1>=j2>=j3>=j4 (and correspondingly permute the input labels). Any zero-sum interaction has j1-j2<=2: the largest magnitude is at most three times the second largest, while a gap >=3 would give a ratio greater than four. For each fixed pair of the smaller frequencies, the sum over the two larger frequencies is bounded by the product of their ell2 norms, since one is a translated reflection of the other. Each small shell contains 2^(j+1) integers. Cauchy-Schwarz on the smaller shells therefore bounds the unweighted four-frequency sum by C*2^((j3+j4)/2)*product_r X_(r,jr). Division by N3>=2^j3 leaves C*2^(-(j3-j4)/2).

Sum F001 with the offset q=j1-j2 in {0,1,2}. Dropping the upper restriction on the small shell indices only increases this positive sum, leaving at most C*(sum_J X_(1,J)X_(2,J-q))*(sum_(ell>=m)2^(-(ell-m)/2)X_(3,ell)X_(4,m)). Interpret negative shell subscripts as zero. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the first factor by ||X_1||_ell2||X_2||_ell2. In the second set r=ell-m, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to each shifted scalar product, and sum the geometric series: its bound is ||X_3||_ell2||X_4||_ell2/(1-2^(-1/2)). Sum over at most 24 shell orderings and three offsets. Since sum_j X_(r,j)^2=||x_r||_ell2^2, this proves the finite estimate. For arbitrary nonnegative square-summable inputs, restrict all four to |k|<=m. The positive sum is the increasing supremum of these finite sums and the restricted norms are bounded by the original norms; taking the supremum proves the infinite estimate. Restricting the positive summation set can only decrease it.

Fix s in [0,1], tau>0, nonnegative n and mean-zero polynomial inputs f1,f2,f3. In each nonzero term of R2 put d=-k, p=a+b, A=|ab|, B0=|cd| and order the four magnitudes. The phase ratios are A/B0 and B0/A. N002 yields |eta|/|k|<=6/N3. Its small-time bound also gives |eta|/(tau|abck|)<=3|p|*min(A,B0)/(A B0)=3|p|/max(A,B0)<=18/N3. The geometric mean with weights 1-s and s is |eta|/(|k|*|abc|^s)<=6^(1-s)*18^s*tau^s/N3. Terms with zero phase or input, or with zero output, contribute zero, so no division by zero is used.

Dualize the R2 formula against an arbitrary ell2 coefficient sequence of norm one, take absolute values and use F001. Apply N003 with the first three sequences |a|^s|hat f1(a)|, |b|^s|hat f2(b)|, |c|^s|hat f3(c)| and the fourth the reflected absolute dual coefficients. Their norms are at most the H^s input norms and one. The prefactor tau/18 gives the asserted tau^(1+s) bound. The time phase and any inserted multiplier of modulus <=1 cannot increase this majorant. This includes each resonant restriction. Trilinearity and the estimate make polynomial approximations Cauchy in L2 and make the limit independent of approximating sequences; this gives the unique bounded trilinear extension.

Now H002 gives 0<gamma<=1. Fix mean-zero w in H^gamma and f in L2, and temporarily assume L1: ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M, delta=||f-w||_2<=1 and 0<tau<=1. F002 with sigma=gamma controls R2(w,w,w) by C M^3 tau^(1+gamma). Telescope R2(f,f,f)-R2(w,w,w) into three trilinear terms with one slot f-w and other slots chosen from f,w. F002 with sigma=0 controls their sum by C tau delta (||f||_2+||w||_2)^2. Since ||f||_2<=M+1, this is at most C_M tau delta, proving the numerical-state estimate. The argument introduces no Sobolev regularity for f. Discharge L1 into the numerical-state bound's antecedent.

Orthogonality of exp(i*k*x) in normalized measure gives the L2 Fourier norm identity on polynomials; completion gives it on L2. Unimodularity and conjugate symmetry of exp(i*t*k^3) give unitarity, reality and mean preservation of S directly in Fourier coefficients. Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||Dinv f||_infty<=(sum_(k!=0)k^(-2))^(1/2)||f||_2, and ||Dinv f||_(H^1)<=sqrt(2)||f||_2. More generally H^1 embeds in L^infty by the same summable reciprocal weights. For A0,B0 in H^1, the product rule together with this embedding gives ||A0 B0||_(H^1)<=C||A0||_(H^1)||B0||_(H^1), first on polynomials and then by density. Apply this to the two inverse derivatives to obtain the J bound. The Fourier coefficient of a product of two L2 functions is bounded by the product of their L2 norms by Cauchy-Schwarz. Therefore ||B_t(f,g)||_(H^(-p_star))^2<=||f||_2^2||g||_2^2 sum_(k!=0) k^2<k>^(-2*p_star), and this series converges because p_star=23/14>3/2. The same coefficient bound with sum k^(-2) gives ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2. On mean-zero coefficients <k>^(-p_star)<=|k|^(-1), so the negative-norm comparison follows. In J_t(A0,B0), bound its first inverse derivative in L2 and its second in L^infty to get the asymmetric bound. All constants are uniform in t since S is an isometry. Bounded-product extensions follow by the displayed estimates and density.

For smooth mean-zero paths f,g the nonzero kth Fourier coefficient of J_t(f,g) is sum_(a+b=k) exp(-i*3*k*a*b*t)(i*a)^(-1)(i*b)^(-1) hat f(a)hat g(b). Differentiating the phase contributes 3*i*k times the product coefficient. Thus partial_t J_t(f,g)=3 B_t(f,g)+J_t(f',g)+J_t(f,g'). Integrate in time and divide by three to obtain the normal-form identity with both endpoints. Smooth spatial Fourier series and their derivatives converge absolutely, justifying the differentiation. J is symmetric. In J_t(B_t(f,g),h), Dinv B_t(f,g)=S_(-t)P[(S_t f)(S_t g)], since Dinv*partial_x=P. Substitution, without commuting any operator through a product, gives the stated Cint identity after integration. The calculation holds on each smooth time piece, so summing preserves both external endpoints. For time-independent f set g=f and divide the integral by two; this yields Stage(t;f)=[J_s(f,f)]/6.

Apply E002 with alpha=0 to arbitrary X paths on I=[a,b], 0<=a<=b, |I|<=1. This is exactly its L^infty L2 and derivative H^(-23/14) hypothesis, and any slot may carry the negative norm. For constant H^s inputs apply its time-independent clause with alpha=s in [0,1]. The source operator C is exactly Cint: e^(t partial_x^3)=S_(-t) and Fourier coefficients, projections and inverse derivatives agree. Every source L2 and H^r norm, and hence X norm, equals sqrt(2*pi) times ours. Dividing the trilinear inequalities by sqrt(2*pi) changes only their constants by 2*pi. Thus both normalized inequalities follow, also for continuous piecewise smooth paths with their weak derivatives.

H002 gives 0<gamma<=1. Apply E003 with sigma=gamma, using epsilon=1/8 at gamma=1/2. Its a(sigma) equals a_gamma; all three cases give 0<=a_gamma<1. This gives ||fg||_2<=C_gamma||f||_(H^gamma)||g||_(H^a_gamma). The bilinear conversion of source norms only changes the constant by sqrt(2*pi).

Choose once and for all 0<epsilon_stage<=1/8 sufficiently small for E004 at sigma=1/2. This choice follows from E004's 'any fixed sufficiently small epsilon>0': the allowed positive epsilons include an interval immediately to the right of zero, which contains a number at most 1/8. Fix this choice independently of the state, norm bound, timestep, step index and spectral support. This auxiliary choice leaves a_gamma=1/8 at gamma=1/2 unchanged. Fix mean-zero w in H^gamma with ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M, 0<tau<=1 and n>=0. Apply E004 with f=g=w, sigma=gamma, beta=a_gamma, and epsilon=epsilon_stage in the midpoint case, uniformly over all times in the step. If 0<gamma<1/2, beta0=2*gamma-3/2, a_gamma-beta0=2-3*gamma>0 and 1+gamma-a_gamma=1/2+2*gamma>0. Its time exponent is (1/2+2*gamma)/(5/2-gamma); subtracting gamma gives (gamma^2-gamma/2+1/2)/(5/2-gamma)>0, since the numerator equals (gamma-1/4)^2+7/16. If gamma=1/2, beta0=-1/2-epsilon_stage<1/8=a_gamma<3/2=1+gamma. The time exponent is (11/8)/(2+epsilon_stage)=11/(16+8*epsilon_stage)>=11/17>1/2=gamma. If 1/2<gamma<=1, beta0=gamma-1<=0=a_gamma<=1+gamma, and the time exponent (1+gamma)/2 is at least gamma. All denominators are positive. Thus in every case the allowed beta yields a power at least gamma. Because 0<tau<=1, replacing that power by gamma enlarges the right side, proving sup_step||Stage(t;w)||_(H^a_gamma)<=C_gamma*M^2*tau^gamma after converting norms. Next apply E004 with the same inputs and beta=1+gamma, retaining epsilon=epsilon_stage at the midpoint. This beta is the included upper endpoint; the denominator is respectively 5/2-gamma, 2+epsilon_stage, or 2, and the numerator is zero. Hence sup_step||Stage(t;w)||_(H^(1+gamma))<=C_gamma*M^2. For either application, dividing the source output norm by sqrt(2*pi) and replacing the two source input norms by sqrt(2*pi) times their normalized norms only changes the constant by sqrt(2*pi). The fixed admissible midpoint choice is absorbed into C_gamma. Both constants therefore have the asserted C_(M,gamma) form and are independent of the step, interval position and spectral support. The arbitrary choices establish the two universal stage bounds, using only the H^gamma regularity of w.

Fix a smooth real mean-zero initial datum and tau>0. All products and Fourier multipliers preserve smoothness and reality. F_tau has P in both terms. H_tau has P in its first term, its second is a scalar mean times S_tau Dinv f, and both endpoint terms have an outer inverse derivative. Thus every iterate stays smooth real and mean zero. At each step take f=S_(-t_n)u^n. Apply E005: v^(n+1)=f+F_n(t_n+tau)+C_n(t_n+tau)-R2_(n,tau)(f,f,f). Here source e^(t partial_x^3)=S_(-t), source A^n=C_n(t_n+tau), and source R2 is D012 with the identical -tau/(18*i*k), covariance and phases. The source physical step agrees term by term with D008-D009, including S_(s-tau) in the last endpoint product.

The Interp formula gives V_n(t_n)=f. At the other endpoint Q_n cancels its part of W_n, leaving F001, so V_n(t_n+tau)=v^(n+1). Thus V is continuous and piecewise smooth and Y_n(t_n)=0. Differentiate the formula: V_n'=B_t(f+F_n,f+F_n)/2-W_n/tau=B_t(z_n,z_n)/2-W_n/tau. Expanding V_n=z_n+Y_n by bilinearity gives V_n'-B_t(V_n,V_n)/2=-B_t(Y_n,z_n)-B_t(Y_n,Y_n)/2-W_n/tau=rho_n'. Concatenating these increments gives the asserted equation and Rres(0)=0.

Fix M>=1, smooth mean-zero f,w and 0<tau<=1, n>=0; assume L1: ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M and delta=||f-w||_2<=1. Put q=tau^gamma+delta<=2. N005 gives F_n(t)=[J_s(f,f)]/6 and hence sup||F_n||_(H^1)<=C_M and sup||F_n-Stage(t;w)||_(H^1)<=C_M delta, by bilinearity and ||f||_2<=M+1. N006 and a_gamma<1 then give ||F_n||_(H^a_gamma)+||F_n||_2<=C_M q. Since z_n'=B_t(f,f)/2, N005 also gives ||z_n||_X<=C_M.

Set A0=Stage(t;w) and D0=F_n-A0. The exact-data square satisfies ||partial_x[(S_t A0)^2]||_2<=2 C_gamma ||A0||_(H^(1+gamma))||A0||_(H^a_gamma)<=C_M tau^gamma, by N006 and the product rule. The difference of squares is (S_t D0) S_t(F_n+A0). Its derivative is bounded in L2 by the H^1 algebra bound of N005 and F001, giving C_M delta. Thus sup||B_t(F_n,F_n)||_2<=C_M q and sup||Q_n||_2<=C_M tau q. Apply the numerical-state clause of N004 to f,w to control R2(f,f,f) by C_M tau q. Therefore ||W_n||_2<=C_M tau q.

Use Dinv B_t(f,F_n)=S_(-t)P[(S_t f)(S_t F_n)]. Split f=w+(f-w). N006 bounds the w-product by C_gamma||w||_(H^gamma)||F_n||_(H^a_gamma)<=C_M q; the other product is <=delta||S_t F_n||_infty<=C_M delta by F001 and N005's H^1 embedding. Hence ||Dinv B_t(f,F_n)||_2<=C_M q. Differentiation gives Y_n'=B_t(f,F_n)+B_t(F_n,F_n)/2-W_n/tau. F002 and boundedness of Dinv on mean-zero L2 yield ||Dinv Y_n'||_2<=C_M q. Integrating from Y_n(t_n)=0 gives ||Dinv Y_n||_2<=C_M tau q.

Apply N005's normal form to C_n with f constant and F_n'=B_t(f,f)/2. As F_n(t_n)=0, C_n(t)=J_t(f,F_n(t))/3-Cint_[t_n,t](f,f,f)/6. The first term is O(q) by F001 and N005. In the cubic integral telescope f around w. N006 with exponent gamma on (w,w,w) gives O(tau^gamma) and with exponent zero on the three difference terms gives O(delta). Therefore ||C_n||_2<=C_M q. F002 and Y_n=C_n+Q_n-(t-t_n)W_n/tau now give ||Y_n||_2<=C_M q. From F003 and the mean-zero comparison ||Y_n||_(H^(-p_star))<=||Dinv Y_n||_2, also applied to Y_n', obtain ||Y_n||_X<=C_M q and ||Y_n||_(H^(-p_star))<=C_M tau q. All output clauses hold under L1. Discharge L1 and universally quantify the data.

Fix arbitrary step data M,f,w,tau,n and assume L1: M>=1, 0<tau<=1, ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M and delta=||f-w||_2<=1. Set q=tau^gamma+delta. Apply N008 to this same Interp tuple. In the first integral of rho_n apply N005's normal form to (Y_n,z_n). The boundary is O(tau q) by ||Dinv Y_n||_2<=C_M tau q, ||z_n||_2<=C_M and the asymmetric J bound. The integral with Y_n' is O(tau q) by ||Dinv Y_n'||_2<=C_M q. In the remaining term z_n'=B_t(f,f)/2, symmetry of J and N005's cubic identity give a constant multiple of Cint(f,f,Y_n). By N006 with the negative norm on Y_n its bound is C tau||f||_X^2||Y_n||_X+C||f||_2^2||Y_n||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M tau q; f is constant so ||f||_X=||f||_2<=M+1.

For the second integral apply N005's normal form to (Y_n,Y_n). Its boundary is <=C||Dinv Y_n||_2||Y_n||_2<=C_M tau q^2, and its differentiated terms have integrals <=C tau||Dinv Y_n'||_2||Y_n||_2<=C_M tau q^2. Since q<=2 this is O(tau q). The affine W_n term is O(tau q) by N008. Thus sup||rho_n||_2<=C_M tau q. Directly in Rres'=-B(Y_n,z_n)-B(Y_n,Y_n)/2-W_n/tau, apply N005's negative-norm product bound and N008's strong bounds and W_n bound, giving ||Rres'||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M(q+q^2)<=C_M q. Both output inequalities hold under L1; discharge L1.

Fix any smooth real mean-zero solution u of u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)*partial_x(u^2) on [0,T], the normalized KdV equation of D020, and define v(t)=S_(-t)u(t). Take its numerical interpolation V with residual Rres. Put M=1+sup||v||_(H^gamma), e=v-V and fix I=[a,b] starting at a grid point, h=b-a<=1, 0<tau<=1. Assume L1: E_I=sup_I||e||_2<=1. At each step intersecting I use f=v^n=V(t_n), w=v(t_n), delta_n=||f-w||_2<=E_I and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n. N007 supplies the actual residual identity and grid values, and N009 gives sup||rho_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n and ||Rres'||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M q_n. There are at most h/tau+1 intersected steps (including a final partial step). Hence sup_(a<=t<=b)||Rres(t)-Rres(a)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). For the exact path, D004 gives partial_t S_(-t)=partial_x^3 S_(-t), commuting with spatial derivatives. Thus v'=S_(-t)(u_t+u_xxx)=(1/2)S_(-t)partial_x(u^2)=(1/2)B_t(v,v), since S_t v=u. Smoothness justifies this differentiation and the spatial products. Subtracting N007's identity V'=B_t(V,V)/2+Rres' and using symmetry and bilinearity gives e'=(B_t(v,v)-B_t(V,V))/2-Rres'=B_t(e,(v+V)/2)-Rres'=B_t(e,v-e/2)-Rres'. N005 then gives ||e||_X(I)<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), and ||v||_X(I)+||V||_X(I)<=C_M. Here V=v-e, and the exact solution has L2 norm <=M throughout.

Define FI(t)=integral_a^t B_s(e,v-e/2)ds. Integration gives e(t)=e(a)+FI(t)-(Rres(t)-Rres(a)). Fix N>=2 only for analysis. For low frequencies N005's bound ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2, followed by two powers of frequency on |k|<=N, gives sup_I||P_(<=N)FI||_2<=C_M N^2 h E_I. For high frequencies apply the normal form in N005 with g=v-e/2, retaining both endpoints. Since e'=B(e,g)-Rres' and g'=B(v,v)/2-B(e,g)/2+Rres'/2, symmetry of J and the cubic identity give exactly FI(t)=[J_s(e,g)]_a^t/3-Cint_[a,t](e,g,V)/3-Cint_[a,t](v,v,e)/6+(1/3)integral_a^t J_s(Rres',V)ds. Indeed g-e/2=V combines the first differentiated pair, and -J(Rres',g)+J(e,Rres')/2=-J(Rres',V) before multiplication by -1/3. N005's H^1 bound on J bounds both high-output endpoints by C_M N^(-1)E_I. This includes the initial endpoint when e(a)!=0.

Let f1,f2,f3 be any three paths of finite X norm on I. For each path decompose frequencies at N/3. If all three input frequencies have modulus <=N/3, their sum has modulus <=N, so that cubic contribution vanishes after P_(>N). Multilinearity writes the remaining contribution as the sum of Cint(P_(>N/3)f1,f2,f3), Cint(P_(<=N/3)f1,P_(>N/3)f2,f3), and Cint(P_(<=N/3)f1,P_(<=N/3)f2,P_(>N/3)f3). Fourier projections contract L2 and the derivative H^(-23/14) norm. Each designated high input has H^(-23/14) norm <=C N^(-23/14) times its L2 norm. N006 therefore bounds this sum by C*h*product_j||f_j||_X+C*N^(-23/14)*product_j||f_j||_(L^infty L2), putting the negative norm on the designated high input in each summand. Instantiate this inequality for (e,g,V) and (v,v,e), where g=v-e/2. F001 gives ||e||_X<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), the other X norms <=C_M, and their L2 products <=C_M E_I. Consequently the two projected cubic integrals have total norm <=C_M*h*tau^gamma+C_M*(h+N^(-23/14))*E_I.

For the forcing term in F002 use the actual stepwise Rres' from N007. On each intersected step define again f=v^n, w=v(t_n), delta_n=||f-w||_2 and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n. On this step the forcing integral is the sum -Cint(Y_n,z_n,V)-Cint(Y_n,Y_n,V)/2-tau^(-1)integral J_s(W_n,V)ds over that intersection. N008 gives ||Y_n||_X<=C_M q_n and ||Y_n||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M tau q_n. N006 with the negative norm on Y_n, and F001's bound on V, control each cubic term by C_M tau q_n; for the term with two Y_n use q_n<=2. N008's ||W_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n and N005's L2 bound for J control the last integral by C_M tau q_n, even on a partial step. Summing yields C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). Together with F002-F003 this gives sup||P_(>N)FI||_2<=C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-p_star))E_I. Add the low-frequency estimate and F001's residual bound in the exact error identity. The result is E_I<=||e(a)||_2+C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(N^2*h+h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-23/14))*E_I. Discharge L1.

Fix a smooth real mean-zero datum u0 and assume L1: ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R. H001-H003 and N001 give a common M bound depending only on T,gamma,R. Take the exact u from N001, put v=S_(-t)u, construct V by Interp, and set e=v-V. N001 identifies u as a smooth solution of u_t+u_xxx=u*u_x=(1/2)*partial_x(u^2) and v=S_(-t)u, so the explicit normalized exact-solution premise of N010 is satisfied. Use N010 with a constant C_M enlarged to work throughout this ball. Define N=ceil(max(2,8*C_M,(8*C_M)^(14/23))). Then C_M(N^(-1)+N^(-23/14))<=1/4. Then choose delta in (0,1] so small that C_M delta(N^2+3)<=1/4, and restrict tau<=delta/2. On any interval starting at a grid point and of length h<=delta with error supremum <=1, N010 absorbs the error coefficient: h+tau<=3delta/2, and hence E_I<=2||e(a)||_2+C'_M delta*tau^gamma. These choices depend only on the common M and gamma,T.

Partition the grid into blocks of floor(delta/tau) steps and a possibly shorter final block. Full block lengths belong to [delta/2,delta], so there are at most 2T/delta+1 blocks. Iterate F001, beginning with e(0)=0, to get sup_[0,t]||e||_2<=K*tau^gamma on every prefix on which ||e||_2<=1; K depends only on T,gamma,R. This includes a prefix ending inside the last step, because N010 explicitly allows a partial final interval. N007 gives continuity of the interpolant; the exact solution is continuous by N001. For contradiction assume L2: the error first reaches one at a time in [0,T]. At that first time, the same finite recurrence through that first time would give <=K*tau^gamma. Choose tau0<=min(1,delta/2) so small that K*tau0^gamma<1/2, possible because H002 gives gamma>0. This contradicts L2, which is discharged; hence the estimate holds on all [0,T]. N007 gives V(t_n)=S_(-t_n)u^n and N001 gives unitarity of the twist, so the grid-point bound follows. No bound depends on higher smooth norms or spectral support. Discharge L1 into the datum-ball antecedent and quantify over all such smooth data.

H001-H003 give the ranges T>0, 0<gamma<=1, R>0. Fix arbitrary real mean-zero u0 in H^gamma and assume L1: ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R. Let u0_m=P_(<=m)u0. The data are real mean-zero Fourier polynomials, ||u0_m||_(H^gamma)<=R, and ||u0_m-u0||_2 tends to zero by the convergent Fourier norm sum. N001 supplies exact solutions u_m,u with a common M bound and sup_[0,T]||u_m-u||_2<=C(T,2R)||u0_m-u0||_2 tending to zero. The solution u has precisely the continuous distributional smooth-approximation convention in the target.

For each fixed tau>0, Psi_tau is continuous from mean-zero L2 to L2. Indeed N005 gives Dinv:L2->H^1 and the H^1 product bound; consequently F_tau:L2->H^1 is a continuous quadratic map. The first term of H_tau is a product of inverse derivatives. Its second has the continuous bilinear scalar mean P0(f^2) multiplied by S_tau Dinv f. Its third is the H^1 product (S_s Dinv f)^3 followed by Dinv. Its fourth is the product of D^(-2)F_tau(f) and Dinv f, with unitary S factors and a final D^(-2). Each is continuous into L2; all scalar coefficients, including tau^(-1), are finite for this fixed tau. Hence the map and all of its finitely many iterates are continuous. The same formulas preserve reality and zero mean: explicit P, outer inverse derivatives, and the zero-mean factor in the scalar-mean term show this directly.

Take C,tau0 from N011, determined only by T,gamma,R. Fix an arbitrary positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0. Applying N011 to u0_m gives the same error bound C*tau^gamma for every m. 1: import Mathlib
2: open scoped BigOperators ENNReal
3: open MeasureTheory Filter Set
4: noncomputable section
5: namespace KdV
6: abbrev Coeff := ℤ → ℂ
7: abbrev Curve := ℝ → Coeff
8: def weight (s : ℝ) (k : ℤ) : ℝ := (1 + (k : ℝ)^2) ^ s
9: def H (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Prop := Summable (fun k => weight s k * ‖f k‖^2)
10: def hn (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : ℝ := Real.sqrt (∑' k, weight s k * ‖f k‖^2)
11: def dh (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Prop :=
12:   f 0 = 0 ∧ Summable (fun k : ℤ => if k = 0 then 0 else |(k : ℝ)|^(2*s) * ‖f k‖^2)
13: def dn (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : ℝ :=
14:   Real.sqrt (∑' k : ℤ, if k = 0 then 0 else |(k : ℝ)|^(2*s) * ‖f k‖^2)
15: def realCoeff (f : Coeff) : Prop := ∀ k, f (-k) = star (f k)
16: def mz (f : Coeff) : Prop := f 0 = 0
17: def data (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Prop := H s f ∧ mz f
18: def rd (s : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Prop := data s f ∧ realCoeff f
19: def smooth (f : Coeff) : Prop := ∀ m : ℕ, H (m : ℝ) f
20: def poly (f : Coeff) : Prop := Set.Finite (Function.support f)
21: def ik (k : ℤ) : ℂ := Complex.I * (k : ℂ)
22: def air (t : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff :=
23:   fun k => Complex.exp (Complex.I * (t : ℂ) * (k : ℂ)^3) * f k
24: def proj (f : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => if k = 0 then 0 else f k
25: def mean (f : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => if k = 0 then f 0 else 0
26: def invD (f : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => if k = 0 then 0 else (ik k)⁻¹ * f k
27: def invD2 (f : Coeff) : Coeff := invD (invD f)
28: def dx (f : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => ik k * f k
29: def mul (f g : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => ∑' a : ℤ, f a * g (k-a)
30: def cube (f : Coeff) : Coeff := mul (mul f f) f
31: def low (N : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff := fun k => if |(k : ℝ)| ≤ N then f k else 0
32: def high (N : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff := f - low N f
33: def eval (f : Coeff) (x : ℝ) : ℂ := ∑' k : ℤ, Complex.exp (Complex.I * (k : ℂ) * (x : ℂ)) * f k
34: def linfty (f : Coeff) : ℝ := sSup ((fun x => ‖eval f x‖) '' Icc 0 (2*Real.pi))
35: def bn (t : ℝ) (f g : Coeff) : Coeff := air (-t) (dx (mul (air t f) (air t g)))
36: def jn (t : ℝ) (f g : Coeff) : Coeff := air (-t) (proj (mul (air t (invD f)) (air t (invD g))))
37: def cint (a b : ℝ) (f g h : Curve) : Coeff :=
38:   fun k => ∫ t in a..b, (air (-t) (proj (mul (proj (mul (air t (f t)) (air t (g t)))) (air t (invD (h t)))))) k
39: def intC (a b : ℝ) (f : Curve) : Coeff := fun k => ∫ t in a..b, f t k
40: def stage (n : ℕ) (τ t : ℝ) (f g : Coeff) : Coeff :=
41:   (1/2 : ℂ) • intC ((n : ℝ)*τ) t (fun r => bn r f g)
42: def favg (τ α : ℝ) : ℂ := (τ : ℂ)⁻¹ * ∫ t in (0 : ℝ)..τ, Complex.exp (-Complex.I * (t : ℂ) * (α : ℂ))
43: def eta (τ α β : ℝ) : ℂ := favg τ (α+β) - favg τ α * favg τ β
44: def phase1 (a b : ℤ) : ℝ := 3*(a:ℝ)*(b:ℝ)*((a+b):ℤ)
45: def phase2 (k c p : ℤ) : ℝ := 3*(k:ℝ)*(c:ℝ)*(p:ℝ)
46: abbrev Mult := ℤ → ℤ → ℤ → ℤ → ℂ
47: def unitMult : Mult := fun _ _ _ _ => 1
48: def rterm (μ : Mult) (n : ℕ) (τ : ℝ) (f g h : Coeff) (k : ℤ) (v : ℤ × ℤ) : ℂ :=
49:   let a := v.1
50:   let b := v.2
51:   let c := k-a-b
52:   let α := phase1 a b
53:   let β := phase2 k c (a+b)
54:   if k = 0 ∨ a+b = 0 then 0 else
55:     -(τ : ℂ)/(18*ik k) * μ k a b c *
56:       Complex.exp (-Complex.I * ((n:ℝ)*τ : ℝ) * ((α+β : ℝ) : ℂ)) *
57:       eta τ α β * f a * g b * h c
58: def rem (μ : Mult) (n : ℕ) (τ : ℝ) (f g h : Coeff) : Coeff :=
59:   fun k => ∑' v : ℤ × ℤ, rterm μ n τ f g h k v
60: def quad (τ : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff :=
61:   (1/6 : ℂ) • proj (mul (air τ (invD f)) (air τ (invD f))) -
62:   (1/6 : ℂ) • air τ (proj (mul (invD f) (invD f)))
63: def cubic (τ : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff :=
64:   let F := quad τ f
65:   let E := fun s => air (τ-s) (invD (cube (air s (invD f))))
66:   let G := fun s => air (τ-s) (invD2 (mul (air (s-τ) (invD2 F)) (air s (invD f))))
67:   (1/3 : ℂ) • proj (mul (air τ (invD f)) (invD F)) +
68:   ((τ/9 : ℝ) : ℂ) • mul (air τ (invD f)) (mean (mul f f)) -
69:   (1/54 : ℂ) • (E τ - E 0) - ((1/(27*τ) : ℝ) : ℂ) • (G τ - G 0)
70: def step (τ : ℝ) (f : Coeff) : Coeff := air τ f + quad τ f + cubic τ f
71: def iter (τ : ℝ) (q : Coeff) : ℕ → Coeff
72:   | 0 => q
73:   | n+1 => step τ (iter τ q n)
74: def pstar : ℝ := 23/14
75: def aux (γ : ℝ) : ℝ := if γ < 1/2 then 1/2-γ else if γ = 1/2 then 1/8 else 0
76: def sourceAux (s ε : ℝ) : ℝ := if s = 0 then 1/2+ε else if s < 1/2 then 1/2-s else if s = 1/2 then ε else 0
77: def beta0 (s ε : ℝ) : ℝ := if s < 1/2 then 2*s-3/2 else if s = 1/2 then -1/2-ε else s-1
78: def k3 (a b c d : ℤ) : ℝ :=

1: Removing the logarithmic loss in the Li–Wu KdV integrator
2: Kaiwen Jin
3: yui.ui.siki@gmail.com
4: 10 October 2026
5: Abstract
6: Li and Wu proved that their unfiltered integrator for periodic KdV converges inL2 with
7: error O(τγ log(1/τ))for real, mean-zero Hγ data,0 <γ≤ 1. We remove the logarithmic factor
8: for the same time-semidiscrete algorithm, with constants uniform on boundedHγ sets. The
9: main estimate concerns the exact averaged cubic remainder. Retaining both ratios of its two
10: oscillatory phases bounds the dual four-frequency multiplier by the reciprocal of the third largest
11: frequency. A dyadic four-linear estimate sums this majorant without a logarithm and includes
12: a mixedL2 endpoint. That endpoint controls the remainder at the numerical state without a
13: numerical Sobolev bound. We then prove the full global estimate using the continuous trilinear
14: bounds of Li and Wu, a stepwise residual calculation, low–high frequency stability, a restarted
15: bootstrap, and density. Finite Fourier experiments check the implemented update, the remainder,
16: and accumulated step defects.
17: 1 Introduction
18: Low spatial regularity limits the accuracy of time discretizations for dispersive equations. For
19: periodic KdV, differentiation in the quadratic nonlinearity makes a directL2 perturbation estimate
20: insufficient. The unfiltered method of Li and Wu integrates the leading oscillatory interactions
21: explicitly and treats its numerical trajectory as a perturbed KdV solution. Their convergence
22: theorem givesCτγ log(1/τ)in L2 forHγ data with0 <γ≤ 1[ 1, Theorem 1.1]. The necessity of the
23: logarithm is left open in [1, Section 11]; this is the fixed-scheme question in AIM problem 518 [3].
24: We prove the boundCτγ for that same method, uniformly on bounded sets of real, mean-zero
25: Hγ data. The improvement comes from the averaging remainder, rather than a change in the update.
26: Its multiplier contains the covariance of two exponential phases. Each phase can be integrated
27: against the other, giving two ratio bounds. Keeping their minimum matters when the output
28: frequency is small. After duality the four frequencies sum to zero, their largest two magnitudes
29: are comparable, and the remaining multiplier is controlled by1/N3, whereN3 is the third largest
30: magnitude. The smaller dyadic scales then carry a summable geometric factor.
31: The resulting trilinear estimate includes exponent zero. This is a local remainder estimate: it
32: does not assert a uniform global rate on anL2 ball. Its role is to compare the cubic remainder at the
33: numerical state with the remainder at an exactHγ state using only theirL2 difference. We retain
34: the continuous trilinear estimates of Li and Wu and give the residual and stability argument in full.
35: In particular, the normal-form identity keeps both endpoints when the time interval is restarted,
36: and its forcing term is estimated from the actual stepwise residual. A fixed-timestep approximation
37: argument then removes the temporary smoothness used in the calculations.
38: The experiments use a fixed finite Fourier cutoff, complete polynomial intermediates, and
39: independently checked reference resolutions. They illustrate the remainder and error accumulation.

For the real mean-zero 2*pi-periodic source equation U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, with normalized homogeneous norms, the following results hold in its norm-preserving twisted representation. For every s>=0, time horizon A>0 and L2 upper bound B0, Galerkin solutions with datum q in dot H^s and ||q||_2<=B0 obey sup_[0,A]||U_m||_(dot H^s)<=M_s, uniformly in m, with M_s depending only on s,A,B0,||q||_(dot H^s). For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,A];H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L^infty dot H^s to a distributional solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e.. This solution is unique, is C([0,A];dot H^s), preserves L2 at every time and depends Lipschitz continuously on the datum for s>1/2, and also for 0<s<=1/2. At s=0 there is a unique C([0,A];L2) solution with Lipschitz dependence obtained by smoothing. For theta in (-1,0] and two data q,r in L2 whose norms sum to at most B0, the two twisted flows satisfy sup_[0,A]||Utw-Vtw||_(dot H^theta)<=C' C_(B0)^A ||q-r||_(dot H^theta), where C',C_(B0) depend only on B0,theta.

Theorem 4.2. Let M0 be given and let s0 ≥ 0. Assume that v(m)(0) = v0 ∈ ˙H s0 and
suppose further that ∥v(m)(0)∥ ˙H 0 ≤ M0. Let T > 0 and let v(m)(t) be a solution of (4.1)
over [0,T ]. Then v(m)(t) solves (4.10) and, uniformly in m, satisﬁes the estimate
∥v(m)(t)∥ ˙H s0 ≤Ms0 for 0 ≤t ≤T, (4.13)
whereMs0 depends only on M0, T , ∥v(0)∥ ˙H s0 and s0.


Theorem 4.3. Let s0 > 0, v(0) ∈ ˙H s0 and let T > 0 be ﬁxed. Let σ be ﬁxed so that
0 < σ < s0. Then there exists a subsequence of v(m)(t) ( which we still label by (m))
of solutions of (4.1), with the same initial data v(0) ∈ ˙H s0, such that v(m)(t) converges
strongly in Lp([0,T ];H σ), for any ﬁxed 1 < p <∞, and ∗-weakly in L∞([0,T ]; ˙H s0) to
v∞(t); and v∞(t) is a solution of (3.8) in the sense of Deﬁnition 3.1 and is bounded in
L∞([0,T ], ˙H s0) with norm
∥v∞∥L∞([0,T ], ˙H s0 ) ≤Ms0, (4.20)
whereMs0 is as in (4.13). Moreover,
∥v∞(t)∥ ˙H 0 = ∥v0∥ ˙H 0 a.e. in [0,T ]. (4.21)


Theorem 5.1. Let s >1/2, v(0) = v0 ∈ ˙H s, and let T > 0 be ﬁxed. Then the solution
v = v∞ of (3.9), in the sense of Deﬁnition 3.1, which was constructed in Theo rem 4.3
is unique. Moreover, the solution is of the class C([0,T ]; ˙H s), and depends Lipschitz
continuously on the initial data in the sense that is describ ed in (5.18) below. Furthermore,

E001.explanation: Fourier identification uses the normalized measure dx/(2π) on the same 2π torus. dh/dn are exactly mean-zero homogeneous H^s membership/norm; contH in the inhomogeneous norm has the identical topology by the two-sided weight comparisons on |k|≥1. The sign=-1 coefficient equation is U_t=UU_x+U_xxx, since (ik)^3=-ik³; twisted (-1) is its norm-preserving e^(+itk³) source twist. bit retains uniform Galerkin bounds and uniform limiting-flow bounds with constants chosen before every datum in the prescribed norm bounds, Galerkin subsequences strongly in each finite L^p H^σ and weak-star in L∞ dot H^s, existence/uniqueness/continuity, conservation, H^s Lipschitz dependence, the s=0 smooth-approximation flow and the full theta∈(-1,0] exponential-in-time dependence. The strong L^p condition is convergence of the integral of the pth power of the norm; weak-star is testing the Fourier dual pairing against every Bochner L¹ dot H^(-s) path. These characterize precisely those convergence modes in the separable weighted ℓ² model, in both directions. A common bound can be enlarged to cover Galerkin and limiting solutions, so separate existential bound variables do not change uniformity. Curves are identified only on the declared horizon. All appearances of exact impose the solution relation rather than assuming it. Reflection/sign transfer to the target is proved in T001, not built into this premise.

E002.explanation: cint is the Fourier form of D015 with both projections and the inverse derivative in the third input; constant paths implement the time-independent clause. srcScale=√(2π) multiplies every normalized H^r or L² norm, including both summands of X, yielding precisely Li-Wu's unnormalized norms. cubicBounds at this scale quantifies alpha∈[0,1], every 0≤a≤b with b-a≤1, and every admissible triple, with the negative-norm factor allowed in each Fin 3 slot and the product over the other two. The first constant is chosen before the interval and paths; the constant-input constant may depend on s. aeH and weakD express the given L∞ regularity and weak time derivative through their absolutely continuous coefficient representatives; changing a representative on a null set does not change any integral or essential norm. Weighted ℓ² separability identifies coordinate measurability plus membership with Bochner measurability. Conversely these norm/weak-derivative data give exactly such representatives. H 0 on the output records that the asserted L² bound is a bound on an actual L² object. Normalization is performed in T006, not silently absorbed by changing this premise.

E003.explanation: Spatial multiplication is convolution of normalized coefficients, with output H 0 membership and the L² estimate both asserted. productBounds retains every sigma∈[0,1] and every fixed epsilon>0; sourceAux is 1/2+epsilon at zero, 1/2-sigma below the midpoint, epsilon at the midpoint, and zero above it. Each norm is multiplied by √(2π), exactly the source normalization. The constant may depend on sigma and the fixed epsilon but is independent of the input functions. This is the same product inequality in both Fourier and physical models, without a mean-zero restriction on either input.

E004.explanation: stage is one half of the coefficient integral of B_s(f,g) from n tau to t. stageBounds preserves all 0<sigma≤1, every beta in the closed interval [beta0,1+sigma], n≥0, tau>0 and the entire step, on time-independent mean-zero H^sigma inputs. beta0 has exactly the three source formulas. At sigma=1/2 the phrase 'any fixed sufficiently small epsilon>0' is encoded as existence of epsilon0>0 followed by every 0<epsilon<epsilon0; its constant may depend on that fixed epsilon and beta, never on the state, n, tau or support. Away from the midpoint beta0 is independent of epsilon and is encoded with epsilon=0 only as an unused argument. The time exponent is exactly (1+sigma-beta)/(1+sigma-beta0) and all norms carry √(2π). The Fourier integral and physical stage agree coefficientwise; the estimate asserts H^beta membership, so it is also the bounded extension described by the source.

E005.explanation: schemeIdentity is the exact source algebraic identity in the common Fourier representation: q=S_(n tau) f, and air(-n tau-tau)(step tau q) is the twisted physical update. quad and cubic expand D008-D009 exactly, including S_(s-tau) in the final endpoint product and the outer inverse second derivative. rem uses zero output at k=0, excludes a+b=0, and has exactly -tau/(18 i k), exp(-i n tau Phi) and eta_tau with alpha=3ab(a+b), beta=3kc(a+b). Summing over a,b with c=k-a-b is a bijective reindexing of a+b+c=k, including all zero input modes, whose phases cancel. The right side is f+Stage+integral B(f,Stage)-R2. Smooth mean-zero inputs, all tau>0 and all natural n are retained, with no support restriction.

P.explanation: Together with H001-H003 the parameters are exactly T>0, 0<gamma≤1 and R>0. rate chooses C>0 and tau0>0 before every real mean-zero H^gamma datum q of norm≤R and before L, so the constants depend only on T,gamma,R. It includes existence and uniqueness, on [0,T], of the continuous H^gamma distributional solution obtained from smooth Fourier-cutoff solutions in uniform L²; uniqueness is in precisely that solution class. For every such solution and every natural L>0 with tau=T/L≤tau0, gridRate asserts H^0 membership of each numerical iterate and the norm error at every n≤L, including n=0. This is equivalent to the displayed maximum over the nonempty finite grid. iter is the explicitly expanded fixed Li-Wu step, with no spatial cutoff and no numerical H^gamma hypothesis. hn 0 is exactly the normalized physical L² norm by the specified Fourier-completion convention; in the other direction each physical datum/solution and scheme has precisely these coefficient sequences and equality/norm bounds. Equation identification uses the coefficient integral formulation of the distributional equation; continuity and L² products justify testing individual modes and recovering all smooth periodic tests. The smooth-approximation convention is witnessed and never made an extra hypothesis on the datum. T012 performs the fixed-timestep limiting argument, preserving the constants and all quantifiers.

For the real mean-zero 2*pi-periodic source equation U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, with normalized homogeneous norms, the following results hold in its norm-preserving twisted representation. For every s>=0, time horizon A>0 and L2 upper bound B0, Galerkin solutions with datum q in dot H^s and ||q||_2<=B0 obey sup_[0,A]||U_m||_(dot H^s)<=M_s, uniformly in m, with M_s depending only on s,A,B0,||q||_(dot H^s). For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,A];H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L^infty dot H^s to a distributional solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e.. This solution is unique, is C([0,A];dot H^s), preserves L2 at every time and depends Lipschitz continuously on the datum for s>1/2, and also for 0<s<=1/2. At s=0 there is a unique C([0,A];L2) solution with Lipschitz dependence obtained by smoothing. For theta in (-1,0] and two data q,r in L2 whose norms sum to at most B0, the two twisted flows satisfy sup_[0,A]||Utw-Vtw||_(dot H^theta)<=C' C_(B0)^A ||q-r||_(dot H^theta), where C',C_(B0) depend only on B0,theta.

Smooth data give spatially smooth solutions on [0,T]. For two real mean-zero L2 data q,r of norms summing to at most B0, the exact solutions satisfy sup_[0,T]||u_q-u_r||_2<=C(T,B0)||q-r||_2. Twisting v(t)=S_(-t)u(t) preserves all Sobolev norms and for smooth data v'=B_t(v,v)/2. Consequently M=1+sup_[0,T]||v||_(H^gamma)<=1+A uniformly on the datum ball.

argument.text: Fix a real mean-zero q in H^gamma and assume L1: ||q||_(H^gamma)<=R. H001-H003 give T>0, 0<gamma<=1 and R>0. Use E001 for source datum U0(x)=-q(-x), exponent s=gamma and horizon T. Reflection and sign preserve the Fourier Sobolev and L2 norms, so ||U0||_(dot H^gamma)<=R and ||U0||_2<=R. The source yields a global unique continuous flow, its uniform Sobolev bound, and smooth flows when the datum is smooth (apply its positive regularity statements for each integer exponent in that case). Its Galerkin bound and limiting-solution bound are uniform for the prescribed norm bounds.

produces.statement: For the source datum U0(x)=-q(-x) there is a unique continuous homogeneous H^gamma source flow U on [0,T], with uniform bound determined only by T,gamma,R; for smooth q it has every Sobolev regularity.

argument.text: Take that source flow U and set u(t,x)=-U(t,-x). At (t,-x), u_t=-U_t, u_x=U_x and u_xxx=U_xxx, so u_t+u_xxx=-U U_x=u*u_x. Fourier coefficients are hat u(k)=-hat U(-k), preserving reality, zero mean and every Fourier norm. On mean-zero functions and s>=0, |k|<=<k><=sqrt(2)|k|, hence ||f||_(dot H^s)<=||f||_(H^s)<=2^(s/2)||f||_(dot H^s); for s<0 the inequalities reverse as in the supplied norm convention. The source bound therefore gives some A(T,gamma,R) in our norm. It also holds for a smooth-approximation limit by passing first in each finite Fourier norm sum and then taking the supremum over finite sets. The sign-reflection map is invertible, so uniqueness and continuous dependence transfer. Finally differentiation of v=S_(-t)u cancels the linear KdV term and yields v'=B_t(v,v)/2 for smooth data; the unimodular Fourier symbol of S preserves all norms. Thus M=1+sup||v||_(H^gamma)<=1+A as asserted. This proves the asserted existence, bound, twist identity and solution convention for arbitrary q under L1; discharge L1.

For arbitrary real mean-zero L2 data q1,q2 and B0>=0, temporarily assume L2: ||q1||_2+||q2||_2<=B0. Apply E001's theta=0 dependence statement at time horizon T to -q1(-x),-q2(-x). Their norms and their difference norm are unchanged. The source twists are unitary, so its dependence bound gives sup_[0,T]||u_q1-u_q2||_2<=C(T,B0)||q1-q2||_2 in physical variables after sign-reflection. Discharge L2.

argument.text: Fix tau>0 and real alpha,beta. If either phase is zero, substitution in eta shows exact cancellation. Otherwise put h(s)=exp(-i*alpha*s)-M_tau(exp(-i*alpha*s)). The covariance is tau^(-1)integral_0^tau h(s)exp(-i*beta*s)ds. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, |exp(-i*alpha*s)-exp(-i*alpha*r)|<=|alpha||s-r|. Averaging in r gives |h(s)|<=tau|alpha|, and consequently |eta|<=tau|alpha|. Interchange alpha,beta to obtain the minimum. Also |h(0)|+|h(tau)|<=tau|alpha| and integral_0^tau|h'(s)|ds=tau|alpha|. Integrating the beta exponential once by parts gives |eta|<=(|h(0)|+|h(tau)|+integral|h'|)/(tau|beta|)<=2|alpha/beta|. Interchanging phases proves the other ratio. These arguments apply to smooth scalar exponentials, so the calculus identities have no limiting issue.

Fix nonzero integer frequencies a,b,c,d with sum zero, order their magnitudes N1>=N2>=N3>=N4, and put A=|ab|, B0=|cd|. Triangle inequality gives N1<=3N2. For the first majorant, if d is among the largest two, min(A/B0,B0/A)<=1 and 1/|d|<=1/N3. Otherwise the two largest are among a,b,c. If they are a,b, use (B0/A)/|d|=|c|/|ab|<=1/N3. If they are a,c, their ratio lies in [1/3,3], giving (1/|d|)min(A/B0,B0/A)<=3 min(|b|/|d|^2,1/|b|)<=3/max(|b|,|d|)=3/N3; the last inequality follows by dividing into |b|<=|d| and its complement. The b,c case is the identical exchange of a,b. For the second majorant, if the largest two lie in a single pair (a,b) or (c,d), the other pair sum has magnitude <=2N3, whereas max(A,B0)>=N1N2>=N3^2. Since a+b=-(c+d), the ratio is <=2/N3. If they lie in different pairs, the third largest is paired with one of them, so max(A,B0)>=N2N3 while |a+b|<=2N1<=6N2. This gives 6/N3. Ties admit any ordering and the cases still exhaust all possibilities.

argument.text: Fix four finitely supported nonnegative sequences x1,x2,x3,x4 on Z\{0}. Decompose each into shells 2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1), j>=0, and let X_(r,j) be its ell2 norm on shell j. Fix one ordering of shell indices j1>=j2>=j3>=j4 (and correspondingly permute the input labels). Any zero-sum interaction has j1-j2<=2: the largest magnitude is at most three times the second largest, while a gap >=3 would give a ratio greater than four. For each fixed pair of the smaller frequencies, the sum over the two larger frequencies is bounded by the product of their ell2 norms, since one is a translated reflection of the other. Each small shell contains 2^(j+1) integers. Cauchy-Schwarz on the smaller shells therefore bounds the unweighted four-frequency sum by C*2^((j3+j4)/2)*product_r X_(r,jr). Division by N3>=2^j3 leaves C*2^(-(j3-j4)/2).

produces.statement: For all j1>=j2>=j3>=j4>=0, with j1-j2<=2, the sum over zero-sum frequencies in the respective four shells of product_r x_r(k_r)/N3(k1,k2,k3,k4) is at most C*2^(-(j3-j4)/2)*product_r X_(r,jr), where N3 is the third largest magnitude.

argument.text: Sum F001 with the offset q=j1-j2 in {0,1,2}. Dropping the upper restriction on the small shell indices only increases this positive sum, leaving at most C*(sum_J X_(1,J)X_(2,J-q))*(sum_(ell>=m)2^(-(ell-m)/2)X_(3,ell)X_(4,m)). Interpret negative shell subscripts as zero. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the first factor by ||X_1||_ell2||X_2||_ell2. In the second set r=ell-m, apply Cauchy-Schwarz to each shifted scalar product, and sum the geometric series: its bound is ||X_3||_ell2||X_4||_ell2/(1-2^(-1/2)). Sum over at most 24 shell orderings and three offsets. Since sum_j X_(r,j)^2=||x_r||_ell2^2, this proves the finite estimate. For arbitrary nonnegative square-summable inputs, restrict all four to |k|<=m. The positive sum is the increasing supremum of these finite sums and the restricted norms are bounded by the original norms; taking the supremum proves the infinite estimate. Restricting the positive summation set can only decrease it.

The geometric mean with weights 1-s and s is |eta|/(|k|*|abc|^s)<=6^(1-s)*18^s*tau^s/N3. Terms with zero phase or input, or with zero output, contribute zero, so no division by zero is used.

argument.text: Dualize the R2 formula against an arbitrary ell2 coefficient sequence of norm one, take absolute values and use F001. Apply N003 with the first three sequences |a|^s|hat f1(a)|, |b|^s|hat f2(b)|, |c|^s|hat f3(c)| and the fourth the reflected absolute dual coefficients. Their norms are at most the H^s input norms and one. The prefactor tau/18 gives the asserted tau^(1+s) bound. The time phase and any inserted multiplier of modulus <=1 cannot increase this majorant. This includes each resonant restriction. Trilinearity and the estimate make polynomial approximations Cauchy in L2 and make the limit independent of approximating sequences; this gives the unique bounded trilinear extension.

argument.text: Now H002 gives 0<gamma<=1. Fix mean-zero w in H^gamma and f in L2, and temporarily assume L1: ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M, delta=||f-w||_2<=1 and 0<tau<=1. argument.text: Orthogonality of exp(i*k*x) in normalized measure gives the L2 Fourier norm identity on polynomials; completion gives it on L2. Unimodularity and conjugate symmetry of exp(i*t*k^3) give unitarity, reality and mean preservation of S directly in Fourier coefficients. Cauchy-Schwarz gives ||Dinv f||_infty<=(sum_(k!=0)k^(-2))^(1/2)||f||_2, and ||Dinv f||_(H^1)<=sqrt(2)||f||_2. More generally H^1 embeds in L^infty by the same summable reciprocal weights. For A0,B0 in H^1, the product rule together with this embedding gives ||A0 B0||_(H^1)<=C||A0||_(H^1)||B0||_(H^1), first on polynomials and then by density. Apply this to the two inverse derivatives to obtain the J bound. The Fourier coefficient of a product of two L2 functions is bounded by the product of their L2 norms by Cauchy-Schwarz. Therefore ||B_t(f,g)||_(H^(-p_star))^2<=||f||_2^2||g||_2^2 sum_(k!=0) k^2<k>^(-2*p_star), and this series converges because p_star=23/14>3/2. The same coefficient bound with sum k^(-2) gives ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2. On mean-zero coefficients <k>^(-p_star)<=|k|^(-1), so the negative-norm comparison follows. In J_t(A0,B0), bound its first inverse derivative in L2 and its second in L^infty to get the asymmetric bound. All constants are uniform in t since S is an isometry. Bounded-product extensions follow by the displayed estimates and density.

For smooth mean-zero paths f,g the nonzero kth Fourier coefficient of J_t(f,g) is sum_(a+b=k) exp(-i*3*k*a*b*t)(i*a)^(-1)(i*b)^(-1) hat f(a)hat g(b). Differentiating the phase contributes 3*i*k times the product coefficient. Thus partial_t J_t(f,g)=3 B_t(f,g)+J_t(f',g)+J_t(f,g'). Integrate in time and divide by three to obtain the normal-form identity with both endpoints. Smooth spatial Fourier series and their derivatives converge absolutely, justifying the differentiation. J is symmetric. In J_t(B_t(f,g),h), Dinv B_t(f,g)=S_(-t)P[(S_t f)(S_t g)], since Dinv*partial_x=P. Substitution, without commuting any operator through a product, gives the stated Cint identity after integration. The calculation holds on each smooth time piece, so summing preserves both external endpoints. For time-independent f set g=f and divide the integral by two; this yields Stage(t;f)=[J_s(f,f)]/6.

For the real mean-zero 2*pi-periodic source equation U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, with normalized homogeneous norms, the following results hold in its norm-preserving twisted representation. For every s>=0, time horizon A>0 and L2 upper bound B0, Galerkin solutions with datum q in dot H^s and ||q||_2<=B0 obey sup_[0,A]||U_m||_(dot H^s)<=M_s, uniformly in m, with M_s depending only on s,A,B0,||q||_(dot H^s). For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,A];H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L^infty dot H^s to a distributional solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e.. This solution is unique, is C([0,A];dot H^s), preserves L2 at every time and depends Lipschitz continuously on the datum for s>1/2, and also for 0<s<=1/2. At s=0 there is a unique C([0,A];L2) solution with Lipschitz dependence obtained by smoothing. For theta in (-1,0] and two data q,r in L2 whose norms sum to at most B0, the two twisted flows satisfy sup_[0,A]||Utw-Vtw||_(dot H^theta)<=C' C_(B0)^A ||q-r||_(dot H^theta), where C',C_(B0) depend only on B0,theta.

source.statement: For the real mean-zero 2*pi-periodic source equation U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, with normalized homogeneous norms, the following results hold in its norm-preserving twisted representation. For every s>=0, time horizon A>0 and L2 upper bound B0, Galerkin solutions with datum q in dot H^s and ||q||_2<=B0 obey sup_[0,A]||U_m||_(dot H^s)<=M_s, uniformly in m, with M_s depending only on s,A,B0,||q||_(dot H^s). For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,A];H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L^infty dot H^s to a distributional solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e.. This solution is unique, is C([0,A];dot H^s), preserves L2 at every time and depends Lipschitz continuously on the datum for s>1/2, and also for 0<s<=1/2. At s=0 there is a unique C([0,A];L2) solution with Lipschitz dependence obtained by smoothing. For theta in (-1,0] and two data q,r in L2 whose norms sum to at most B0, the two twisted flows satisfy sup_[0,A]||Utw-Vtw||_(dot H^theta)<=C' C_(B0)^A ||q-r||_(dot H^theta), where C',C_(B0) depend only on B0,theta.

argument.text: Apply E002 with alpha=0 to arbitrary X paths on I=[a,b], 0<=a<=b, |I|<=1. This is exactly its L^infty L2 and derivative H^(-23/14) hypothesis, and any slot may carry the negative norm. For constant H^s inputs apply its time-independent clause with alpha=s in [0,1]. The source operator C is exactly Cint: e^(t partial_x^3)=S_(-t) and Fourier coefficients, projections and inverse derivatives agree. Every source L2 and H^r norm, and hence X norm, equals sqrt(2*pi) times ours. Dividing the trilinear inequalities by sqrt(2*pi) changes only their constants by 2*pi. Thus both normalized inequalities follow, also for continuous piecewise smooth paths with their weak derivatives.

H002 gives 0<gamma<=1. Apply E003 with sigma=gamma, using epsilon=1/8 at gamma=1/2. Its a(sigma) equals a_gamma; all three cases give 0<=a_gamma<1. This gives ||fg||_2<=C_gamma||f||_(H^gamma)||g||_(H^a_gamma). The bilinear conversion of source norms only changes the constant by sqrt(2*pi).

Choose once and for all 0<epsilon_stage<=1/8 sufficiently small for E004 at sigma=1/2. This choice follows from E004's 'any fixed sufficiently small epsilon>0': the allowed positive epsilons include an interval immediately to the right of zero, which contains a number at most 1/8. Fix this choice independently of the state, norm bound, timestep, step index and spectral support. This auxiliary choice leaves a_gamma=1/8 at gamma=1/2 unchanged. Fix mean-zero w in H^gamma with ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M, 0<tau<=1 and n>=0. Apply E004 with f=g=w, sigma=gamma, beta=a_gamma, and epsilon=epsilon_stage in the midpoint case, uniformly over all times in the step. If 0<gamma<1/2, beta0=2*gamma-3/2, a_gamma-beta0=2-3*gamma>0 and 1+gamma-a_gamma=1/2+2*gamma>0. Its time exponent is (1/2+2*gamma)/(5/2-gamma); subtracting gamma gives (gamma^2-gamma/2+1/2)/(5/2-gamma)>0, since the numerator equals (gamma-1/4)^2+7/16. If gamma=1/2, beta0=-1/2-epsilon_stage<1/8=a_gamma<3/2=1+gamma. The time exponent is (11/8)/(2+epsilon_stage)=11/(16+8*epsilon_stage)>=11/17>1/2=gamma. If 1/2<gamma<=1, beta0=gamma-1<=0=a_gamma<=1+gamma, and the time exponent (1+gamma)/2 is at least gamma. All denominators are positive. Thus in every case the allowed beta yields a power at least gamma. Because 0<tau<=1, replacing that power by gamma enlarges the right side, proving sup_step||Stage(t;w)||_(H^a_gamma)<=C_gamma*M^2*tau^gamma after converting norms. Next apply E004 with the same inputs and beta=1+gamma, retaining epsilon=epsilon_stage at the midpoint. This beta is the included upper endpoint; the denominator is respectively 5/2-gamma, 2+epsilon_stage, or 2, and the numerator is zero. Hence sup_step||Stage(t;w)||_(H^(1+gamma))<=C_gamma*M^2. For either application, dividing the source output norm by sqrt(2*pi) and replacing the two source input norms by sqrt(2*pi) times their normalized norms only changes the constant by sqrt(2*pi). 25: /-
26: ## Definitions
27: -/
28: namespace Real
29: variable {x y z : ℝ}
30: 
31: /-- The real power function `x ^ y`, defined as the real part of the complex power function.
32: For `x > 0`, it is equal to `exp (y log x)`. For `x = 0`, one sets `0 ^ 0=1` and `0 ^ y=0` for
33: `y ≠ 0`. For `x < 0`, the definition is somewhat arbitrary as it depends on the choice of a complex
34: determination of the logarithm. With our conventions, it is equal to `exp (y log x) cos (π y)`. -/
35: noncomputable def rpow (x y : ℝ) :=
36:   ((x : ℂ) ^ (y : ℂ)).re
37: 
38: noncomputable instance : Pow ℝ ℝ := ⟨rpow⟩
39: 
40: @[simp]
41: theorem rpow_eq_pow (x y : ℝ) : rpow x y = x ^ y := rfl
42: 
43: theorem rpow_def (x y : ℝ) : x ^ y = ((x : ℂ) ^ (y : ℂ)).re := rfl
44: 
45: theorem rpow_def_of_nonneg {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 ≤ x) (y : ℝ) :
46:     x ^ y = if x = 0 then if y = 0 then 1 else 0 else exp (log x * y) := by
47:   simp only [rpow_def, Complex.cpow_def]; split_ifs <;>
48:   simp_all [(Complex.ofReal_log hx).symm, -Complex.ofReal_mul,
49:       (Complex.ofReal_mul _ _).symm, Complex.exp_ofReal_re, Complex.ofReal_eq_zero]
50: 
51: theorem rpow_def_of_pos {x : ℝ} (hx : 0 < x) (y : ℝ) : x ^ y = exp (log x * y) := by
52:   rw [rpow_def_of_nonneg (le_of_lt hx), if_neg (ne_of_gt hx)]
53: 
54: theorem exp_mul (x y : ℝ) : exp (x * y) = exp x ^ y := by rw [rpow_def_of_pos (exp_pos _), log_exp]
55: 
56: @[simp, norm_cast]
57: theorem rpow_intCast (x : ℝ) (n : ℤ) : x ^ (n : ℝ) = x ^ n := by
58:   simp only [rpow_def, ← Complex.ofReal_zpow, Complex.cpow_intCast, Complex.ofReal_intCast,
59:     Complex.ofReal_re]
60: 
61: @[simp, norm_cast]
62: theorem rpow_natCast (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : x ^ (n : ℝ) = x ^ n := by simpa using rpow_intCast x n
63: 
64: @[simp, norm_cast]
65: theorem rpow_neg_natCast (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : x ^ (-n : ℝ) = x ^ (-n : ℤ) := by
66:   rw [← rpow_intCast, Int.cast_neg, Int.cast_natCast]
67: 
68: @[simp]
69: lemma rpow_ofNat (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) [n.AtLeastTwo] :
70:     x ^ (ofNat(n) : ℝ) = x ^ (ofNat(n) : ℕ) :=
71:   rpow_natCast x n
72: 
73: @[simp]
74: theorem rpow_neg_ofNat (x : ℝ) (n : ℕ) [n.AtLeastTwo] : x ^ (-ofNat(n) : ℝ) = x ^ (-ofNat(n) : ℤ) :=
75:   rpow_neg_natCast _ _
76: 
77: @[simp]
78: theorem exp_one_rpow (x : ℝ) : exp 1 ^ x = exp x := by rw [← exp_mul, one_mul]
79: 
80: @[simp] lemma exp_one_pow (n : ℕ) : exp 1 ^ n = exp n := by rw [← rpow_natCast, exp_one_rpow]
81: 
82: theorem rpow_eq_zero_iff_of_nonneg (hx : 0 ≤ x) : x ^ y = 0 ↔ x = 0 ∧ y ≠ 0 := by
83:   simp only [rpow_def_of_nonneg hx]
84:   split_ifs <;> simp [*, exp_ne_zero]
85: 
86: @[simp]
87: lemma rpow_eq_zero (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hy : y ≠ 0) : x ^ y = 0 ↔ x = 0 := by
88:   simp [rpow_eq_zero_iff_of_nonneg, *]
89: 
90: lemma rpow_ne_zero (hx : 0 ≤ x) (hy : y ≠ 0) : x ^ y ≠ 0 ↔ x ≠ 0 := by
91:   simp [hx, hy]
92: 
93: open Real
94: 
95: theorem rpow_def_of_neg {x : ℝ} (hx : x < 0) (y : ℝ) : x ^ y = exp (log x * y) * cos (y * π) := by
96:   rw [rpow_def, Complex.cpow_def, if_neg]
97:   · have : Complex.log x * y = ↑(log (-x) * y) + ↑(y * π) * Complex.I := by
98:       simp only [Complex.log, Complex.norm_real, norm_eq_abs, abs_of_neg hx, log_neg_eq_log,
99:         Complex.arg_ofReal_of_neg hx, Complex.ofReal_mul]

argument.text: Fix any smooth real mean-zero solution u of u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)*partial_x(u^2) on [0,T], the normalized KdV equation of D020, and define v(t)=S_(-t)u(t). Take its numerical interpolation V with residual Rres. Put M=1+sup||v||_(H^gamma), e=v-V and fix I=[a,b] starting at a grid point, h=b-a<=1, 0<tau<=1. Assume L1: E_I=sup_I||e||_2<=1. At each step intersecting I use f=v^n=V(t_n), w=v(t_n), delta_n=||f-w||_2<=E_I and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n. N007 supplies the actual residual identity and grid values, and N009 gives sup||rho_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n and ||Rres'||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M q_n. There are at most h/tau+1 intersected steps (including a final partial step). Hence sup_(a<=t<=b)||Rres(t)-Rres(a)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). For the exact path, D004 gives partial_t S_(-t)=partial_x^3 S_(-t), commuting with spatial derivatives. Thus v'=S_(-t)(u_t+u_xxx)=(1/2)S_(-t)partial_x(u^2)=(1/2)B_t(v,v), since S_t v=u. Smoothness justifies this differentiation and the spatial products. Subtracting N007's identity V'=B_t(V,V)/2+Rres' and using symmetry and bilinearity gives e'=(B_t(v,v)-B_t(V,V))/2-Rres'=B_t(e,(v+V)/2)-Rres'=B_t(e,v-e/2)-Rres'. N005 then gives ||e||_X(I)<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), and ||v||_X(I)+||V||_X(I)<=C_M. Here V=v-e, and the exact solution has L2 norm <=M throughout.

produces.statement: sup_I||Rres(t)-Rres(a)||_2<=C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I), ||e||_X(I)<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), and ||v||_X(I)+||V||_X(I)<=C_M.

argument.text: Define FI(t)=integral_a^t B_s(e,v-e/2)ds. Integration gives e(t)=e(a)+FI(t)-(Rres(t)-Rres(a)). Fix N>=2 only for analysis. For low frequencies N005's bound ||Dinv P(FG)||_2<=C||F||_2||G||_2, followed by two powers of frequency on |k|<=N, gives sup_I||P_(<=N)FI||_2<=C_M N^2 h E_I. For high frequencies apply the normal form in N005 with g=v-e/2, retaining both endpoints. Since e'=B(e,g)-Rres' and g'=B(v,v)/2-B(e,g)/2+Rres'/2, symmetry of J and the cubic identity give exactly FI(t)=[J_s(e,g)]_a^t/3-Cint_[a,t](e,g,V)/3-Cint_[a,t](v,v,e)/6+(1/3)integral_a^t J_s(Rres',V)ds. Indeed g-e/2=V combines the first differentiated pair, and -J(Rres',g)+J(e,Rres')/2=-J(Rres',V) before multiplication by -1/3. N005's H^1 bound on J bounds both high-output endpoints by C_M N^(-1)E_I. This includes the initial endpoint when e(a)!=0.

produces.statement: e(t)=e(a)+FI(t)-(Rres(t)-Rres(a)); sup_I||P_(<=N)FI||_2<=C_M N^2 h E_I; FI(t)=[J_s(e,g)]_a^t/3-Cint_[a,t](e,g,V)/3-Cint_[a,t](v,v,e)/6+(1/3)integral_a^t J_s(Rres',V)ds, with g=v-e/2, and the high-output endpoint norm is <=C_M N^(-1)E_I.

argument.text: Let f1,f2,f3 be any three paths of finite X norm on I. For each path decompose frequencies at N/3. If all three input frequencies have modulus <=N/3, their sum has modulus <=N, so that cubic contribution vanishes after P_(>N). Multilinearity writes the remaining contribution as the sum of Cint(P_(>N/3)f1,f2,f3), Cint(P_(<=N/3)f1,P_(>N/3)f2,f3), and Cint(P_(<=N/3)f1,P_(<=N/3)f2,P_(>N/3)f3). Fourier projections contract L2 and the derivative H^(-23/14) norm. Each designated high input has H^(-23/14) norm <=C N^(-23/14) times its L2 norm. N006 therefore bounds this sum by C*h*product_j||f_j||_X+C*N^(-23/14)*product_j||f_j||_(L^infty L2), putting the negative norm on the designated high input in each summand. Instantiate this inequality for (e,g,V) and (v,v,e), where g=v-e/2. F001 gives ||e||_X<=C_M(tau^gamma+E_I), the other X norms <=C_M, and their L2 products <=C_M E_I. Consequently the two projected cubic integrals have total norm <=C_M*h*tau^gamma+C_M*(h+N^(-23/14))*E_I.

For the forcing term in F002 use the actual stepwise Rres' from N007. On each intersected step define again f=v^n, w=v(t_n), delta_n=||f-w||_2 and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n. On this step the forcing integral is the sum -Cint(Y_n,z_n,V)-Cint(Y_n,Y_n,V)/2-tau^(-1)integral J_s(W_n,V)ds over that intersection. N008 gives ||Y_n||_X<=C_M q_n and ||Y_n||_(L^infty H^(-p_star))<=C_M tau q_n. N006 with the negative norm on Y_n, and F001's bound on V, control each cubic term by C_M tau q_n; for the term with two Y_n use q_n<=2. N008's ||W_n||_2<=C_M tau q_n and N005's L2 bound for J control the last integral by C_M tau q_n, even on a partial step. Summing yields C_M(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). Together with F002-F003 this gives sup||P_(>N)FI||_2<=C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-p_star))E_I. Add the low-frequency estimate and F001's residual bound in the exact error identity. The result is E_I<=||e(a)||_2+C_M(h+tau)tau^gamma+C_M(N^2*h+h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-23/14))*E_I. Discharge L1.

Define N=ceil(max(2,8*C_M,(8*C_M)^(14/23))) for the enlarged uniform stability constant C_M.
Choose delta=min(1,1/(4*C_M*(N^2+3))), decreasing if needed.
Take u from N001 for the current smooth datum.

argument.text: Fix a smooth real mean-zero datum u0 and assume L1: ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R. H001-H003 and N001 give a common M bound depending only on T,gamma,R. Take the exact u from N001, put v=S_(-t)u, construct V by Interp, and set e=v-V. N001 identifies u as a smooth solution of u_t+u_xxx=u*u_x=(1/2)*partial_x(u^2) and v=S_(-t)u, so the explicit normalized exact-solution premise of N010 is satisfied. Use N010 with a constant C_M enlarged to work throughout this ball. Define N=ceil(max(2,8*C_M,(8*C_M)^(14/23))). Then C_M(N^(-1)+N^(-23/14))<=1/4. Then choose delta in (0,1] so small that C_M delta(N^2+3)<=1/4, and restrict tau<=delta/2. On any interval starting at a grid point and of length h<=delta with error supremum <=1, N010 absorbs the error coefficient: h+tau<=3delta/2, and hence E_I<=2||e(a)||_2+C'_M delta*tau^gamma. These choices depend only on the common M and gamma,T.

produces.statement: For the current smooth datum, exact path v and interpolant V, with e=v-V, the fixed N,delta depend only on T,gamma,R. For every positive timestep theta<=delta/2 and every I=[a,b] starting at a grid point with b-a<=delta, if E_I=sup_I||e||_2<=1 then E_I<=2||e(a)||_2+C'_M*delta*theta^gamma.

argument.text: Partition the grid into blocks of floor(delta/tau) steps and a possibly shorter final block. Full block lengths belong to [delta/2,delta], so there are at most 2T/delta+1 blocks. Iterate F001, beginning with e(0)=0, to get sup_[0,t]||e||_2<=K*tau^gamma on every prefix on which ||e||_2<=1; K depends only on T,gamma,R. This includes a prefix ending inside the last step, because N010 explicitly allows a partial final interval. N007 gives continuity of the interpolant; the exact solution is continuous by N001. For contradiction assume L2: the error first reaches one at a time in [0,T]. At that first time, the same finite recurrence through that first time would give <=K*tau^gamma. Choose tau0<=min(1,delta/2) so small that K*tau0^gamma<1/2, possible because H002 gives gamma>0. This contradicts L2, which is discharged; hence the estimate holds on all [0,T]. N007 gives V(t_n)=S_(-t_n)u^n and N001 gives unitarity of the twist, so the grid-point bound follows. No bound depends on higher smooth norms or spectral support. Discharge L1 into the datum-ball antecedent and quantify over all such smooth data.
